Q: Standardized color names? A:

I'm aware this thread is ancient, but Google still redirects here; for the benefit of those who come here from the future, as of 2026, the official standard for CSS3 (CSS Color Module Level 3, W3C Recommendation 18 January 2022) lists the specification for colour names to be used with HTML5/CSS3/SVG. As @Renan explained, the name/colour assignment deliberately matches what the X Window System uses (the first popular graphical web browser, NCSA Mosaic, was initially available on Unix machines).

However, these 'standard' colour names are by no means the only way of describing colours — especially because there are so few of them in the official specifications. These days, since you can use 16 million colours safely enough, listing them all by name is virtually impossible.

But since humans can't distinguish so many different colours, there have always been attempts to categorise the most important distinctions (as judged by humans, not machines) into unique names (or numbers). Commercial colour catalogues such as PANTONE® have been around for aeons, but the Pantone colour names and correspondent sRGB values are considered to be protected by corporate secrecy laws. An alternative convention comes from a popular manufacturer of paints, Resene, from New Zealand, which has published its own list so that people can order the precise tint from their products. They publish their list under a very permissive licence.

Similarly, and also with a permissive licence, the US Military & Bureaucracy publishes their own naming convention as well: U.S. Federal Standard 595C1 - Colors Used In Government Procurement ... but you'll have to convert CIELab colours to sRGB for the table above to make sense to a web browser!

For example, the reddish colour used to paint the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco, CA and the Tagus Bridge in Lisbon, Portugal is known as International Orange (also known as Army-Navy Aeronautical Bulletin (ANA) Paint Color 508 — a colour model used by US military aircraft until 1970).

From the above table, under daylight, this colour would be rendered as #c24e3a, looking like this:

Of course, outside the Web universe, the question of assigning names to colours has been thoroughly researched. Here is a very long list of possible colour name assignments: https://people.csail.mit.edu/jaffer/Color/Dictionaries#Names (kudos to Aubrey Jaffer, who compiled that list as part of her long academic work on colour)

Q: Fastest hash function for a sparse key A:

Such simple code will likely not be space efficient, and your memory access time will likely dominate the time taken to calculate the hash. Since you only have 360 keys, you could list them in order in an array and find the required index quickly with a binary search. Then your main lookup array will be small and more likely to be cached, hence faster. Unless your processor is a potato and your memory is really fast, I suggest you broaden and quantify your requirement about accessing your lookup table beyond cycles to calculate the hash.
